title: Κικόνες καὶ Λωτοφάγοι
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Answering Alcinous, Odysseus praises the feast and the singer, then names himself for the first time to his Phaeacian hosts: he lives on rocky, far-out Ithaca, and no land is sweeter, not even the beds of Calypso and Circe, who both wanted him for a husband. He begins the tale of his homecoming. The wind from Troy brings him to the Cicones at Ismarus, where he sacks a city; his men ignore his warning to leave, feast on the shore, and are routed by the Cicones' neighbours, losing six men from each ship. A storm sent by Zeus shreds the sails, and a north wind then drives him past Cythera for nine days to the land of the Lotus-eaters, whose fruit makes men forget their homecoming. He drags back the scouts who ate it and hurries the rest to the oars.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: τόν is the pronoun 'him', object of προσέφη 'addressed'; ἀπαμειβόμενος 'answering' is the participle of ἀπαμείβομαι, the verb of reply, and πολύμητις 'of many wiles' is built on μῆτις 'cunning intelligence'. Ὀδυσσεύς has the double σ here; Homer writes Ὀδυσ- or Ὀδυσσ- as the verse needs. The line is the narrator's, so it carries no quotation mark, and the raised point after the name hands the floor to Odysseus, who is replying to Alcinous. The speech begins with the next line.

sentences.t:
Ἀλκίνοε κρεῖον, πάντων ἀριδείκετε λαῶν,
ἦ τοι μὲν τόδε καλὸν ἀκουέμεν ἐστὶν ἀοιδοῦ
τοιοῦδ’ οἷος ὅδ’ ἐστί, θεοῖς ἐναλίγκιος αὐδήν.
sentences.tr:
Alkinoe kreion, pantōn arideikete laōn,
ē toi men tode kalon akouemen estin aoidou
toioud’ hoios hod’ esti, theois enalinkios audēn.
sentences.l:
“Alcinous, lord, most conspicuous of all the people,
truly, this is a fine thing, to listen to a minstrel
such as this one is, one like the gods in voice.
sentences.i: “Alcinous, my lord, most distinguished of all the people, it is indeed a fine thing to listen to a minstrel such as this man is, one whose voice is like the gods’.
sentences.n: Ἀλκίνοε and κρεῖον are vocatives: κρεῖον is from κρείων 'lord, ruler', a participle in form, and ἀριδείκετε from ἀριδείκετος, a compliment 'most conspicuous'. λαῶν is a genitive plural in the older shape (Attic λεῶν), partitive after πάντων. ἦ τοι μέν is emphatic, 'truly, indeed'. ἀκουέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν (Attic ἀκούειν) after καλόν. θεοῖς ἐναλίγκιος takes the dative 'like the gods', and αὐδήν is an accusative of respect, 'in voice'. The minstrel is the singer whom the guests have just heard. This is the speech's first line: the Greek prints no quotation marks, and Odysseus goes on speaking well beyond this part.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐγώ γέ τί φημι τέλος χαριέστερον εἶναι
ἢ ὅτ’ ἐυφροσύνη μὲν ἔχῃ κάτα δῆμον ἅπαντα,
sentences.tr:
ou gar egō ge ti phēmi telos chariesteron einai
ē hot’ eyphrosynē men echēi kata dēmon hapanta,
sentences.l:
For I, at least, say there is no fulfilment more pleasing
than when good cheer holds all the land throughout,
sentences.i: For I say there is no fulfilment more pleasing than when good cheer holds the whole land,
sentences.n: The period runs six lines, so it is cut at the comma after ἅπαντα, where the ὅτε-clauses pause. οὐ … φημι is 'I say that … not': the negative belongs to the infinitive clause. τέλος is 'end, fulfilment', the goal of a good life. χαριέστερον is the comparative of χαρίεις 'pleasing'. ἔχῃ is a subjunctive, and ὅτε with the subjunctive names a general situation, 'whenever'. κάτα is accented because it follows its verb: it is either tmesis for κατέχῃ 'holds' or κατά with δῆμον ἅπαντα, 'throughout the whole land', which the rendering follows. ἐυφροσύνη is 'good cheer', and δῆμος here is the land and its people.

sentences.t:
δαιτυμόνες δ’ ἀνὰ δώματ’ ἀκουάζωνται ἀοιδοῦ
ἥμενοι ἑξείης, παρὰ δὲ πλήθωσι τράπεζαι
σίτου καὶ κρειῶν, μέθυ δ’ ἐκ κρητῆρος ἀφύσσων
οἰνοχόος φορέῃσι καὶ ἐγχείῃ δεπάεσσι·
sentences.tr:
daitymones d’ ana dōmat’ akouazōntai aoidou
hēmenoi hexeiēs, para de plēthōsi trapezai
sitou kai kreiōn, methy d’ ek krētēros aphyssōn
oinochoos phoreēisi kai encheiēi depaessi·
sentences.l:
and feasters throughout the halls listen to a minstrel,
sitting in a row, and beside them the tables are filled
with bread and meats, and wine from the mixing-bowl drawing
the cupbearer carries round and pours into the cups;
sentences.i: and the feasters throughout the halls listen to a minstrel, sitting in a row, and the tables beside them are laden with bread and meats, and the cupbearer draws wine from the mixing-bowl and carries it round and pours it into the cups;
sentences.n: Four more subjunctives go with the ὅτε of the last unit: ἀκουάζωνται 'listen', πλήθωσι 'are full' (πλήθω), and φορέῃσι 'carries round', with the ending -ῃσι in place of Attic -ῃ; ἐγχείῃ is 'pours in'. Read the four lines as one sweep of a banquet. σίτου is bread or grain-food and κρειῶν the uncontracted genitive plural of κρέας 'meat'. The κρητήρ is the mixing-bowl in which wine was blended with water, and the οἰνοχόος 'wine-pourer' draws it out (ἀφύσσων). δεπάεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι, and δώματ’ is δώματα 'halls', with its final vowel elided.

sentences.t: τοῦτό τί μοι κάλλιστον ἐνὶ φρεσὶν εἴδεται εἶναι.
sentences.tr: touto ti moi kalliston eni phresin eidetai einai.
sentences.l: This, to me, in my mind appears to be most beautiful.
sentences.i: To my mind this seems the most beautiful thing there is.
sentences.n: τοῦτο 'this' gathers up the whole banquet of the last two units. τί is the enclitic 'somehow' and μοι is 'to me'. κάλλιστον is the superlative of καλός, and εἴδεται is a middle of εἴδομαι 'appear, seem', related to εἶδος 'look'. ἐνὶ φρεσί is 'in my mind': ἐνί is ἐν, and φρεσί is the dative plural of φρήν, here the seat of judgment.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ ἐμὰ κήδεα θυμὸς ἐπετράπετο στονόεντα
εἴρεσθ’, ὄφρ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον ὀδυρόμενος στεναχίζω·
sentences.tr:
soi d’ ema kēdea thymos epetrapeto stonoenta
eiresth’, ophr’ eti mallon odyromenos stenachizō·
sentences.l:
But to you my sorrows, full-of-groaning, your heart was inclined
to ask, so that I may groan the more, lamenting;
sentences.i: But your heart has turned to ask about my sorrows, so full of groaning, so that I shall lament and groan the more;
sentences.n: σοί is a dative of the person whose heart it is, 'to you … your heart'; ἐπετράπετο is the aorist middle of ἐπιτρέπω, 'turned to, gave itself over to'. εἴρεσθ’ is the infinitive of εἴρομαι 'ask' (Attic ἐρέσθαι), and κήδεα 'sorrows' is the uncontracted plural (Attic κήδη). στονόεντα 'full of groaning' comes from στόνος. ὄφρα 'so that' takes the short-vowel subjunctive στεναχίζω, which looks like an indicative. ὀδυρόμενος 'lamenting' is the middle participle of ὀδύρομαι.

sentences.t: τί πρῶτόν τοι ἔπειτα, τί δ’ ὑστάτιον καταλέξω;
sentences.tr: ti prōton toi epeita, ti d’ hystation katalexō;
sentences.l: What first to you, then, and what last shall I recount?
sentences.i: What shall I tell you first, then, and what last?
sentences.n: The question is deliberative: καταλέξω is an aorist subjunctive with a short vowel, 'what am I to recount?', from καταλέγω 'tell in order'. τοι is the enclitic 'to you', and ἔπειτα 'next, then'. πρῶτον 'first' and ὑστάτιον 'last' balance each other, a storyteller's worry about where to begin.

sentences.t: κήδε’ ἐπεί μοι πολλὰ δόσαν θεοὶ Οὐρανίωνες.
sentences.tr: kēde’ epei moi polla dosan theoi Ouraniōnes.
sentences.l: sorrows, since to me many the gods gave, the children-of-Heaven.
sentences.i: since the gods, the children of Heaven, gave me so many sorrows.
sentences.n: κήδε’ is κήδεα, standing in apposition to the τί of the question just asked ('what? sorrows'). δόσαν is the unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι (Attic ἔδοσαν), and πολλά, 'many', is its object, with κήδεα understood. Οὐρανίωνες is formed from Οὐρανός 'Heaven' and means 'descendants of Uranus'; 'dwellers in heaven' is the other ancient reading. ἐπεί gives the reason for the question just asked.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ὄνομα πρῶτον μυθήσομαι, ὄφρα καὶ ὑμεῖς
εἴδετ’, ἐγὼ δ’ ἂν ἔπειτα φυγὼν ὕπο νηλεὲς ἦμαρ
ὑμῖν ξεῖνος ἔω καὶ ἀπόπροθι δώματα ναίων.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ onoma prōton mythēsomai, ophra kai hymeis
eidet’, egō d’ an epeita phygōn hypo nēlees ēmar
hymin xeinos eō kai apoprothi dōmata naiōn.
sentences.l:
But now my name first I shall tell, so that you too
may know, and I, then, having escaped the pitiless day,
to you a guest-friend may be, even far off dwelling in a house.
sentences.i: But now I will tell you my name first, so that you too may know it, and so that I, once I have escaped the pitiless day, may be a guest-friend to you, though I live in a house far away.
sentences.n: μυθήσομαι is the future of μυθέομαι 'tell'. Both εἴδετ’ and ἔω are short-vowel subjunctives after ὄφρα, 'that you may know' (Attic εἰδῆτε) and 'that I may be' (Attic ὦ). φυγὼν ὕπο νηλεὲς ἦμαρ has the preverb ὕπο standing apart from its verb (tmesis for ὑποφυγών): 'having escaped the pitiless day', the day of death; νηλεής is 'pitiless'. ξεῖνος is the person bound by hospitality, host or guest, so 'guest-friend'. ἀπόπροθι is 'far away' (-θι 'at a place'). He asks for a bond that will hold at a distance.

sentences.t:
εἴμ’ Ὀδυσεὺς Λαερτιάδης, ὃς πᾶσι δόλοισιν
ἀνθρώποισι μέλω, καί μευ κλέος οὐρανὸν ἵκει.
sentences.tr:
eim’ Odyseus Laertiadēs, hos pasi doloisin
anthrōpoisi melō, kai meu kleos ouranon hikei.
sentences.l:
I am Odysseus, son-of-Laertes, who by all tricks
to men am a concern, and my fame heaven reaches.
sentences.i: I am Odysseus, son of Laertes, a concern to men for all my tricks, and my fame reaches heaven.
sentences.n: εἴμ’ is εἰμί 'I am', elided. Ὀδυσεύς has a single σ. Λαερτιάδης is a patronymic, 'son of Laertes'. δόλοισιν is a dative plural in -οισιν, 'by tricks'; μέλω with the dative means 'I am a care, a concern, to', and whether the concern is admiring or anxious is left open. πᾶσι agrees with δόλοισιν, 'by every kind of trick'. μευ is μου. κλέος, from κλύω 'hear', is what is heard about a man, his fame, and ἵκει 'reaches' is from ἱκνέομαι. The man is named for the first time in his own voice.

sentences.t: ναιετάω δ’ Ἰθάκην ἐυδείελον·
sentences.tr: naietaō d’ Ithakēn eydeielon·
sentences.l: And I dwell in Ithaca, clear-seen;
sentences.i: And I live in clear-seen Ithaca;
sentences.n: ναιετάω is the uncontracted form (Attic ναιετῶ) and takes the accusative Ἰθάκην 'I inhabit Ithaca'. ἐυδείελον, 'clear-seen', is disputed: the ancients derived it either from δείελος 'evening' or from δῆλος 'visible', and the rendering keeps the literal, second sense. The unit ends mid-line at the raised point.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ὄρος αὐτῇ
Νήριτον εἰνοσίφυλλον, ἀριπρεπές·
sentences.tr:
en d’ oros autēi
Nēriton einosiphyllon, ariprepes·
sentences.l:
and on it a mountain,
Neriton, leaf-shaking, outstanding;
sentences.i: on it there is a mountain, Neriton, leaf-shaking and outstanding;
sentences.n: ἐν is an adverb, 'on it', and αὐτῇ is the dative 'on the island'; there is no verb, 'there is' being understood. Νήριτον is the mountain's name. εἰνοσίφυλλον 'leaf-shaking' is built on ἔνοσις 'shaking' and φύλλον 'leaf', with the first syllable lengthened for the verse. ἀριπρεπές 'outstanding' is from the intensive ἀρι- and πρέπω 'be conspicuous'.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ νῆσοι
πολλαὶ ναιετάουσι μάλα σχεδὸν ἀλλήλῃσι,
Δουλίχιόν τε Σάμη τε καὶ ὑλήεσσα Ζάκυνθος.
sentences.tr:
amphi de nēsoi
pollai naietaousi mala schedon allēlēisi,
Doulichion te Samē te kai hylēessa Zakynthos.
sentences.l:
and around it islands
many are inhabited, very near one another,
Dulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus.
sentences.i: and around it many islands lie inhabited, very close to one another: Dulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus.
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ δέ 'and around' (ἀμφί as an adverb). ναιετάουσι is uncontracted, 'are inhabited', the verb for a place where people live. ἀλλήλῃσι is a dative plural in -ῃσι (Attic ἀλλήλαις), and σχεδόν is 'near'. The three names stand in apposition to νῆσοι, joined by τε … τε καί. ὑλήεσσα 'wooded' is the feminine of ὑλήεις, with -εσσα.

sentences.t:
αὐτὴ δὲ χθαμαλὴ πανυπερτάτη εἰν ἁλὶ κεῖται
πρὸς ζόφον, αἱ δέ τ’ ἄνευθε πρὸς ἠῶ τ’ ἠέλιόν τε,
τρηχεῖ’, ἀλλ’ ἀγαθὴ κουροτρόφος·
sentences.tr:
autē de chthamalē panypertatē ein hali keitai
pros zophon, hai de t’ aneuthe pros ēō t’ ēelion te,
trēchei’, all’ agathē kourotrophos·
sentences.i: It itself lies low, farthest out in the sea toward the western dark, while the others lie apart toward the dawn and the sun; it is rough, but a good nurse of young men;
sentences.n: αὐτή is Ithaca itself, against the neighbouring islands. The sense of πανυπερτάτη is uncertain: 'uppermost of all' may mean 'farthest out to sea' or 'highest'; the rendering takes the first. εἰν ἁλί is ἐν ἁλί, 'in the salt sea'. ζόφος is the murk of the west and ἠῶ τ’ ἠέλιόν τε 'dawn and the sun' the east, so the others lie apart toward the east. τρηχεῖ’ is τρηχεῖα 'rough', agreeing with αὐτή. κουροτρόφος 'nurse of young men' comes from κοῦρος and τρέφω.

sentences.t:
οὔ τοι ἐγώ γε
ἧς γαίης δύναμαι γλυκερώτερον ἄλλο ἰδέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
ou toi egō ge
hēs gaiēs dynamai glykerōteron allo idesthai.
sentences.l:
for not, indeed, I, at least,
than my own land can anything else sweeter see.
sentences.i: for I can see nothing else sweeter than my own land.
sentences.n: οὔ τοι is 'no indeed' and ἐγώ γε 'I at least'. ἧς γαίης is a genitive of comparison, 'than my own land', and ἧς is the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν, here 'my own', easily mistaken for the relative. γλυκερώτερον ἄλλο is 'anything else sweeter'. ἰδέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of εἶδον 'see', dependent on δύναμαι.

sentences.t:
ἦ μέν μ’ αὐτόθ’ ἔρυκε Καλυψώ, δῖα θεάων,
ἐν σπέσσι γλαφυροῖσι, λιλαιομένη πόσιν εἶναι·
sentences.tr:
ē men m’ autoth’ eryke Kalypsō, dia theaōn,
en spessi glaphyroisi, lilaiomenē posin einai·
sentences.l:
Truly me right there held back Calypso, heavenly-one of goddesses,
in hollow caves, yearning for me to be her husband;
sentences.i: Truly, Calypso, heavenly even among goddesses, kept me back there in her hollow caves, yearning to have me for her husband;
sentences.n: ἦ μέν is 'truly, indeed'; μ’ is με 'me'. αὐτόθ’ is αὐτόθι 'right there' (-θι 'at a place'). ἔρυκε is an unaugmented imperfect, 'kept back, held'. δῖα θεάων and ἐν σπέσσι γλαφυροῖσι are stock phrases and are translated the same each time: θεάων is an uncontracted genitive plural (Attic θεῶν), σπέσσι the dative plural of σπέος 'cave', and the plural stands for one dwelling. πόσις is 'husband'. The Greek does not say 'me'; the pronoun has to be supplied for λιλαιομένη πόσιν εἶναι, 'longing that (I) be (her) husband'.

sentences.t:
ὣς δ’ αὔτως Κίρκη κατερήτυεν ἐν μεγάροισιν
Αἰαίη δολόεσσα, λιλαιομένη πόσιν εἶναι·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ autōs Kirkē katerētyen en megaroisin
Aiaiē doloessa, lilaiomenē posin einai·
sentences.l:
And just so Circe held me back in her halls,
the Aeaean, guileful, yearning for me to be her husband;
sentences.i: And in just the same way Circe of Aeaea, the guileful, held me back in her halls, yearning to have me for her husband;
sentences.n: ὣς δ’ αὔτως is 'and in just the same way'. κατερήτυεν is the imperfect of κατερητύω 'hold back', kin to ἔρυκε in the last unit. ἐν μεγάροισιν is a dative plural in -οισιν, plural for one hall. Αἰαίη is the adjective 'of Aeaea', Circe's island, and δολόεσσα 'guileful' the feminine of δολόεις, from δόλος 'trick'. The last phrase repeats the one before word for word.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἐμὸν οὔ ποτε θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἔπειθον.
sentences.tr: all’ emon ou pote thymon eni stēthessin epeithon.
sentences.l: but my heart never in my breast did they persuade.
sentences.i: but they never persuaded the heart in my breast.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ is ἀλλά. ἔπειθον is an imperfect, 'they were trying to persuade', which says they did not succeed; the subject, the two goddesses, is not repeated. ἐμὸν … θυμόν is 'my heart', θυμός being heart or spirit, the seat of feeling and will. ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσιν, 'in my breast'.

sentences.t:
ὣς οὐδὲν γλύκιον ἧς πατρίδος οὐδὲ τοκήων
γίγνεται, εἴ περ καί τις ἀπόπροθι πίονα οἶκον
γαίῃ ἐν ἀλλοδαπῇ ναίει ἀπάνευθε τοκήων.
sentences.tr:
hōs ouden glykion hēs patridos oude tokēōn
gignetai, ei per kai tis apoprothi piona oikon
gaiēi en allodapēi naiei apaneuthe tokēōn.
sentences.l:
So nothing sweeter than one’s own fatherland and than parents
is, even if someone far away a rich house
in a foreign land dwells, apart from his parents.
sentences.i: So nothing is sweeter than one’s own fatherland and parents, even if a man far away dwells in a rich house in a foreign land, apart from his parents.
sentences.n: The accented ὥς is 'so, thus': it draws a general conclusion from the two cases just given. γλύκιον is a comparative, 'sweeter' (Attic γλυκύτερον). ἧς πατρίδος is 'one's own fatherland', the possessive ὅς again, and τοκήων is the Homeric genitive plural of τοκεύς 'parent' (Attic τοκέων). εἴ περ καί τις 'even if anyone'. ἀπόπροθι and ἀπάνευθε 'far away' and 'apart from' echo one another. ἀλλοδαπός means 'belonging to another place'.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἄγε τοι καὶ νόστον ἐμὸν πολυκηδέ’ ἐνίσπω,
ὅν μοι Ζεὺς ἐφέηκεν ἀπὸ Τροίηθεν ἰόντι.
sentences.tr:
ei d’ age toi kai noston emon polykēde’ enispō,
hon moi Zeus epheēken apo Troiēthen ionti.
sentences.l:
But come, to you also my homecoming, full-of-sorrows, let me tell,
which to me Zeus sent, as from Troy I was going.
sentences.i: But come, let me tell you also of my homecoming, so full of sorrows, which Zeus sent upon me as I left Troy.
sentences.n: εἰ δ’ ἄγε is 'come now', an invitation. ἐνίσπω is an aorist subjunctive of ἐννέπω with a short vowel, 'let me tell'. πολυκηδέ’ is πολυκηδέα, from πολύς and κῆδος 'sorrow', agreeing with νόστον 'homecoming'. Here ὅν is the relative 'which', referring to νόστον; it is spelled exactly like the possessive ὅν and the two must be told apart by sense. ἐφέηκεν is ἐπέηκεν 'sent upon', from ἐφίημι. Τροίηθεν is 'from Troy' (-θεν, Ionic η), and ἰόντι a dative participle agreeing with μοι.

sentences.t:
Ἰλιόθεν με φέρων ἄνεμος Κικόνεσσι πέλασσεν,
Ἰσμάρῳ.
sentences.tr:
Iliothen me pherōn anemos Kikonessi pelassen,
Ismarōi.
sentences.l:
From Ilios me bearing, a wind to the Cicones brought near,
to Ismarus.
sentences.i: A wind bearing me from Ilios brought me near the Cicones, to Ismarus.
sentences.n: Ἰλιόθεν is 'from Ilios' (-θεν), Ilios being another name of Troy. με φέρων 'bearing me' has ἄνεμος 'a wind' as its subject. Κικόνεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι, 'the Cicones', a people the poem has not yet introduced. πέλασσεν is the unaugmented aorist of πελάζω 'bring near'. Ἰσμάρῳ 'Ismarus' is in apposition, the place on their coast where the next line has Odysseus sack a city. A new paragraph begins: the tale proper starts here.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δ’ ἐγὼ πόλιν ἔπραθον, ὤλεσα δ’ αὐτούς·
sentences.tr: entha d’ egō polin eprathon, ōlesa d’ autous·
sentences.l: There I the city sacked, and destroyed them;
sentences.i: There I sacked the city and destroyed its people;
sentences.n: ἔπραθον is the aorist of πέρθω 'sack' and ὤλεσα the aorist of ὄλλυμι, here transitive 'destroy'. αὐτούς 'them themselves' means the men of the city, as against the buildings and goods. Odysseus says it briefly and in the first person.

sentences.t:
ἐκ πόλιος δ’ ἀλόχους καὶ κτήματα πολλὰ λαβόντες
δασσάμεθ’, ὡς μή τίς μοι ἀτεμβόμενος κίοι ἴσης.
sentences.tr:
ek polios d’ alochous kai ktēmata polla labontes
dassameth’, hōs mē tis moi atembomenos kioi isēs.
sentences.l:
out of the city wives and many possessions taking
we shared out, so that no man, for me, cheated, should go off short of an equal share.
sentences.i: Taking wives and many possessions out of the city, we shared them out, so that no man, on my account, should go away cheated of an equal share.
sentences.n: ἐκ πόλιος: πόλις has the genitive πόλιος in Homer (Attic πόλεως). ἀλόχους 'wives' are taken with the goods, and the text does not soften it. δασσάμεθ’ is the aorist middle of δατέομαι 'divide among ourselves'. ἀτεμβόμενος is a rare participle, 'deprived, cheated', with the genitive ἴσης, 'of an equal (share)', the noun being understood. κίοι is the optative of κίω 'go', and μοι is 'for me, on my account': the leader's fairness is the point.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἦ τοι μὲν ἐγὼ διερῷ ποδὶ φευγέμεν ἡμέας
ἠνώγεα, τοὶ δὲ μέγα νήπιοι οὐκ ἐπίθοντο.
sentences.tr:
enth’ ē toi men egō dierōi podi pheugemen hēmeas
ēnōgea, toi de mega nēpioi ouk epithonto.
sentences.l:
Then indeed I, on a nimble foot, to flee us
was urging, but they, greatly foolish, did not obey.
sentences.i: Then I, for my part, urged us to flee on nimble feet, but they, great fools, did not obey.
sentences.n: ἠνώγεα is the pluperfect of ἀνώγω 'urge, command', used with the sense of an imperfect. φευγέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν (Attic φεύγειν), with ἡμέας (Attic ἡμᾶς) as its subject. The meaning of διερῷ ποδί is not certain: διερός is guessed to mean 'living, lively' (hence 'nimble') or 'wet'; the rendering takes the first and the phrase means 'quickly'. τοί is the pronoun 'they'. νήπιοι is 'fools', literally 'without sense', and μέγα 'greatly' strengthens it. ἐπίθοντο is the aorist middle of πείθομαι 'obey' (the augmented form; the unaugmented is πίθοντο).

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δὲ πολλὸν μὲν μέθυ πίνετο, πολλὰ δὲ μῆλα
ἔσφαζον παρὰ θῖνα καὶ εἰλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς·
sentences.tr:
entha de pollon men methy pineto, polla de mēla
esphazon para thina kai eilipodas helikas bous·
sentences.l:
And there much wine was being drunk, and many sheep
they were slaughtering by the shore and rolling-gaited, crumple-horned cattle;
sentences.i: There much wine was drunk, and they slaughtered many sheep by the shore, and the cattle of rolling gait and crumpled horn;
sentences.n: μέθυ is the old word for wine, neuter, and πίνετο a passive imperfect, 'was being drunk'. ἔσφαζον 'they were slaughtering' has no subject expressed, the men. μῆλα are sheep or goats. παρὰ θῖνα is 'along the shore'. εἰλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς is a formula: εἰλίποδας describes the cattle's rolling walk, and ἕλικας 'twisted' probably their horns, though the sense is not certain. The men are feasting where they have just plundered, and the line ends at a raised point.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δ’ ἄρ’ οἰχόμενοι Κίκονες Κικόνεσσι γεγώνευν,
οἵ σφιν γείτονες ἦσαν, ἅμα πλέονες καὶ ἀρείους,
ἤπειρον ναίοντες, ἐπιστάμενοι μὲν ἀφ’ ἵππων
ἀνδράσι μάρνασθαι καὶ ὅθι χρὴ πεζὸν ἐόντα.
sentences.tr:
tophra d’ ar’ oichomenoi Kikones Kikonessi gegōneun,
hoi sphin geitones ēsan, hama pleones kai areious,
ēpeiron naiontes, epistamenoi men aph’ hippōn
andrasi marnasthai kai hothi chrē pezon eonta.
sentences.l:
Meanwhile, having gone, Cicones to Cicones were calling out,
who were their neighbours, both more numerous and stronger,
the mainland dwelling, knowing how from horses
with men to fight, and where it is needful, on foot being.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the Cicones had gone off and were calling to other Cicones, their neighbours, who lived inland, more numerous and stronger, and skilled at fighting men from horses and, where need be, on foot.
sentences.n: τόφρα is 'meanwhile'. οἰχόμενοι 'going off' is from οἴχομαι, and γεγώνευν an imperfect of γεγωνέω 'shout so as to be heard'. Κίκονες Κικόνεσσι sets the two groups side by side. οἵ σφιν γείτονες ἦσαν is 'who were their neighbours'; ἀρείους is the comparative ἀρείων 'better, stronger'. ἤπειρον ναίοντες is 'dwelling on the mainland', that is inland. ἐπιστάμενοι takes an infinitive, 'knowing how to', and ἀφ’ ἵππων is 'from horses': the Greek does not say whether from horseback or from chariots. ὅθι χρή 'where it is needful'; πεζὸν ἐόντα 'being on foot' (ἐόντα = ὄντα).

sentences.t:
ἦλθον ἔπειθ’ ὅσα φύλλα καὶ ἄνθεα γίγνεται ὥρῃ,
ἠέριοι·
sentences.tr:
ēlthon epeith’ hosa phylla kai anthea gignetai hōrēi,
ēerioi·
sentences.l:
They came then, as many as leaves and flowers come to be in season,
early;
sentences.i: Then they came, as many as the leaves and flowers that grow in their season, early in the morning;
sentences.n: ἔπειθ’ is ἔπειτα. In ὅσα φύλλα καὶ ἄνθεα γίγνεται a neuter plural takes a singular verb, and the clause is a comparison of number: the Cicones were as many as leaves and flowers in their season. ὥρῃ is a dative of time with Ionic η. The meaning of ἠέριοι is uncertain: 'early in the morning' (from ἠώς or ἦρι) is the usual guess, and 'in the mist' (from ἠήρ) has also been proposed; 'early' is used. The unit ends mid-line at the raised point.

sentences.t:
τότε δή ῥα κακὴ Διὸς αἶσα παρέστη
ἡμῖν αἰνομόροισιν, ἵν’ ἄλγεα πολλὰ πάθοιμεν.
sentences.tr:
tote dē rha kakē Dios aisa parestē
hēmin ainomoroisin, hin’ algea polla pathoimen.
sentences.l:
then indeed an evil portion of Zeus stood by
to us, dread-fated, so that many pains we might suffer.
sentences.i: Then, to us so grimly fated, an evil portion from Zeus stood by, that we might suffer many pains.
sentences.n: ῥα is a worn-down ἄρα. αἶσα is 'portion, lot', and the genitive Διός says whose: Odysseus puts the disaster in Zeus's allotment. παρέστη is the aorist of παρίστημι 'stand beside'. αἰνομόροισιν is a dative plural in -οισιν, 'to us the dread-fated', from αἰνός 'dread' and μόρος 'portion'. ἵν’ is ἵνα 'so that', and with the optative πάθοιμεν it gives a purpose set in the past.

sentences.t:
στησάμενοι δ’ ἐμάχοντο μάχην παρὰ νηυσὶ θοῇσι,
βάλλον δ’ ἀλλήλους χαλκήρεσιν ἐγχείῃσιν.
sentences.tr:
stēsamenoi d’ emachonto machēn para nēusi thoēisi,
ballon d’ allēlous chalkēresin encheiēisin.
sentences.l:
And having taken their stand, they fought a fight beside the swift ships,
and they hurled at one another with bronze-fitted spears.
sentences.i: They took their stand and fought a battle beside the swift ships, and hurled bronze-fitted spears at one another.
sentences.n: στησάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ἵστημι, 'having taken position'. ἐμάχοντο μάχην 'fought a fight' is a cognate accusative. νηυσί is a dative plural of ναῦς, and θοῇσι a dative plural in -ῃσι. βάλλον is an imperfect, 'were hurling at'. χαλκήρεσιν ἐγχείῃσιν is a dative plural, -ῃσιν being the ending of ἐγχείη 'spear' (kin to ἔγχος), and χαλκήρης means 'fitted with bronze'.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα μὲν ἠὼς ἦν καὶ ἀέξετο ἱερὸν ἦμαρ,
τόφρα δ’ ἀλεξόμενοι μένομεν πλέονάς περ ἐόντας.
sentences.tr:
ophra men ēōs ēn kai aexeto hieron ēmar,
tophra d’ alexomenoi menomen pleonas per eontas.
sentences.l:
As long as it was morning and the sacred day was growing,
during that time, defending ourselves, we stood firm, though more they were.
sentences.i: For as long as it was morning and the sacred day was growing, for that time we stood our ground and warded them off, though they were the more numerous.
sentences.n: ὄφρα … τόφρα is a pair: 'as long as … for that time'. ἠώς is the Ionic form of the word for dawn or morning, and ἦν is 'was'. ἀέξετο is the imperfect middle of ἀέξω 'grow, increase'. ἱερὸν ἦμαρ is a fixed phrase: ἱερός is 'sacred', as elsewhere in the poem, though here it may mean 'strong', the day in its strength. ἀλεξόμενοι 'warding off' comes from ἀλέξω, and μένομεν is 'we stood our ground'. In πλέονάς περ ἐόντας, περ makes the participle concessive, 'though they were more'.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠέλιος μετενίσσετο βουλυτόνδε,
καὶ τότε δὴ Κίκονες κλῖναν δαμάσαντες Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ēelios metenisseto boulytonde,
kai tote dē Kikones klinan damasantes Achaious.
sentences.l:
But when the sun was moving over toward the ox-unyoking time,
then indeed the Cicones turned the Achaeans, having overpowered them.
sentences.i: But when the sun turned toward the time for unyoking oxen, then at last the Cicones overpowered the Achaeans and made them give way.
sentences.n: ἦμος is 'when' (epic; Attic ὅτε). ἠέλιος is the sun, and μετενίσσετο 'was moving over' comes from μετανίσσομαι. βουλυτόνδε has the -δε of direction and names the hour when oxen are unyoked, late afternoon. κλῖναν is the aorist of κλίνω 'bend, turn', and in battle it means to make the enemy give way. δαμάσαντες is the aorist participle of δαμάζω 'overpower'. Odysseus' men are called Ἀχαιοί, 'Achaeans', like the Greeks at Troy.

sentences.t:
ἓξ δ’ ἀφ’ ἑκάστης νηὸς ἐυκνήμιδες ἑταῖροι
ὤλονθ’· οἱ δ’ ἄλλοι φύγομεν θάνατόν τε μόρον τε.
sentences.tr:
hex d’ aph’ hekastēs nēos eyknēmides hetairoi
ōlonth’· hoi d’ alloi phygomen thanaton te moron te.
sentences.l:
And six from each ship, well-greaved companions,
perished; but the rest of us fled both death and doom.
sentences.i: Six well-greaved companions from each ship perished; the rest of us escaped death and doom.
sentences.n: ἐυκνήμιδες is a stock epithet, 'well-greaved', translated whenever it appears; greaves guard the shins. ἀφ’ ἑκάστης νηός is 'from each ship'. ὤλονθ’ is ὤλοντο with the τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of οἱ. οἱ δ’ ἄλλοι is 'the others', meaning us. φύγομεν is unaugmented (Attic ἐφύγομεν). θάνατόν τε μόρον τε is one idea in two nouns, 'death and doom'; μόρος is a person's allotted portion.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν δὲ προτέρω πλέομεν ἀκαχήμενοι ἦτορ,
ἄσμενοι ἐκ θανάτοιο, φίλους ὀλέσαντες ἑταίρους.
sentences.tr:
enthen de proterō pleomen akachēmenoi ētor,
asmenoi ek thanatoio, philous olesantes hetairous.
sentences.l:
From there farther we sailed, grieved in heart,
glad to be out of death, dear companions having lost.
sentences.i: From there we sailed on, grieved at heart, glad to be out of death, though we had lost our dear companions.
sentences.n: ἔνθεν is 'from there' (-θεν), and προτέρω 'farther on'. ἀκαχήμενοι ἦτορ is the perfect participle of ἀχέω 'grieve' with ἦτορ as an accusative of respect, 'grieved in heart'. ἄσμενοι ἐκ θανάτοιο, 'glad to be out of death', has a genitive in -οιο. φίλους ὀλέσαντες ἑταίρους is 'having lost dear companions'. Gladness at escape and grief for the dead stand side by side. A new paragraph begins.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα μοι προτέρω νῆες κίον ἀμφιέλισσαι,
πρίν τινα τῶν δειλῶν ἑτάρων τρὶς ἕκαστον ἀῦσαι,
οἳ θάνον ἐν πεδίῳ Κικόνων ὕπο δῃωθέντες.
sentences.tr:
oud’ ara moi proterō nēes kion amphielissai,
prin tina tōn deilōn hetarōn tris hekaston aysai,
hoi thanon en pediōi Kikonōn hypo dēiōthentes.
sentences.l:
And not then for me farther went the ships, both-sides-curving,
before someone each of the miserable companions three times had called,
who died on the plain, by the Cicones cut down.
sentences.i: And my ships, curved on both sides, would not go on before someone had called three times on each of the miserable companions who died there on the plain, cut down by the Cicones.
sentences.n: κίον is 'went' (κίω), without augment. ἀμφιέλισσαι is disputed: 'curved at both ends' or 'rowed on both sides'; the rendering keeps 'both-sides-curving'. πρίν with the infinitive ἀῦσαι means 'before … had called': τινα is the indefinite subject, 'someone', and ἕκαστον, partitive with τῶν δειλῶν ἑτάρων, is its object. δειλός is 'miserable, poor'. τρίς 'three times': calling the dead by name three times was a rite of farewell, and the poem assumes it is known. θάνον is an unaugmented aorist of θνῄσκω. δῃωθέντες is the aorist passive participle of δῃόω 'cut down', and Κικόνων ὕπο shows anastrophe.

sentences.t:
νηυσὶ δ’ ἐπῶρσ’ ἄνεμον Βορέην νεφεληγερέτα Ζεὺς
λαίλαπι θεσπεσίῃ, σὺν δὲ νεφέεσσι κάλυψε
γαῖαν ὁμοῦ καὶ πόντον·
sentences.tr:
nēusi d’ epōrs’ anemon Boreēn nephelēgereta Zeus
lailapi thespesiēi, syn de nepheessi kalypse
gaian homou kai ponton·
sentences.i: Zeus who gathers the clouds stirred up the North Wind against my ships in a wondrous squall, and with clouds hid land and sea alike;
sentences.n: νηυσί is a dative, 'against the ships'. ἐπῶρσ’ is ἐπῶρσε, the aorist of ἐπόρνυμι 'rouse against'. Βορέης 'the North Wind' is here a named wind, in apposition to ἄνεμον. νεφεληγερέτα is the short-α nominative of Zeus's title, from νεφέλη 'cloud' and ἀγείρω 'gather'. λαίλαπι θεσπεσίῃ is 'with a wondrous squall': λαῖλαψ is a sudden storm, θεσπέσιος 'wondrous'. σὺν … κάλυψε is tmesis for συγκάλυψε 'covered over', with νεφέεσσι, a dative plural in -εσσι. The unit ends mid-line at the raised point.

sentences.t: ὀρώρει δ’ οὐρανόθεν νύξ.
sentences.tr: orōrei d’ ouranothen nyx.
sentences.l: and night had sprung up from the sky.
sentences.i: and night had sprung up out of the sky.
sentences.n: ὀρώρει is the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι 'rouse; intransitive, arise', with the sense 'had sprung up'. οὐρανόθεν is 'from the sky' (-θεν). The darkness comes from the cloud that Zeus has spread over earth and sea.

sentences.t:
αἱ μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἐφέροντ’ ἐπικάρσιαι, ἱστία δέ σφιν
τριχθά τε καὶ τετραχθὰ διέσχισεν ἲς ἀνέμοιο.
sentences.tr:
hai men epeit’ epheront’ epikarsiai, histia de sphin
trichtha te kai tetrachtha dieschisen is anemoio.
sentences.l:
They then were carried aslant, and their sails
in three and in four pieces split the force of the wind.
sentences.i: Then the ships were carried on aslant, and the force of the wind split their sails into three and four pieces.
sentences.n: αἱ μέν is 'they', the ships. ἐφέροντ’ is ἐφέροντο 'were carried'. ἐπικάρσιαι is uncertain: 'slantwise, aslant' and 'head first' (from κάρ-, 'head') are both guessed, and the sense is not known; 'aslant' is used. σφιν is 'their', a dative of the possessor. τριχθά τε καὶ τετραχθά are adverbs in -χθά, 'in three parts and in four'. ἲς ἀνέμοιο is 'the force of the wind', a genitive in -οιο, and διέσχισεν 'split apart'.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐς νῆας κάθεμεν, δείσαντες ὄλεθρον,
αὐτὰς δ’ ἐσσυμένως προερέσσαμεν ἤπειρόνδε.
sentences.tr:
kai ta men es nēas kathemen, deisantes olethron,
autas d’ essymenōs proeressamen ēpeironde.
sentences.l:
And these into the ships we let down, fearing destruction,
but the ships themselves, hurriedly, we rowed forward toward the mainland.
sentences.i: We let the sails down into the ships, fearing destruction, and rowed the ships themselves on in haste toward land.
sentences.n: τά is the pronoun 'these', the sails. κάθεμεν is the aorist of καθίημι, 'we let down', without augment. δείσαντες is the aorist participle of δείδω 'fear'. αὐτάς is the ships themselves, feminine plural. ἐσσυμένως 'in haste' comes from ἐσσύμενος 'hurrying', a participle of σεύομαι. προερέσσαμεν is 'we rowed forward', and ἤπειρόνδε has the -δε of direction, 'toward the mainland'.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δύω νύκτας δύο τ’ ἤματα συνεχὲς αἰεὶ
κείμεθ’, ὁμοῦ καμάτῳ τε καὶ ἄλγεσι θυμὸν ἔδοντες.
sentences.tr:
entha dyō nyktas dyo t’ ēmata syneches aiei
keimeth’, homou kamatōi te kai algesi thymon edontes.
sentences.l:
There two nights and two days continuously, always,
we lay, together with weariness and with pains eating our hearts.
sentences.i: There we lay for two nights and two days without a break, eating our hearts out with weariness and pain.
sentences.n: δύω and δύο are two spellings of 'two', side by side; ἦμαρ has the plural ἤματα. συνεχὲς αἰεί is 'continuously, without stopping'. κείμεθ’ is κείμεθα 'we lay'. καμάτῳ is a dative of κάματος 'weariness' and ἄλγεσι a dative plural in -εσι. θυμὸν ἔδοντες, 'eating our hearts', is an idiom for wasting away with distress.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τρίτον ἦμαρ ἐυπλόκαμος τέλεσ’ Ἠώς,
ἱστοὺς στησάμενοι ἀνά θ’ ἱστία λεύκ’ ἐρύσαντες
ἥμεθα, τὰς δ’ ἄνεμός τε κυβερνῆταί τ’ ἴθυνον.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē triton ēmar eyplokamos teles’ Ēōs,
histous stēsamenoi ana th’ histia leuk’ erysantes
hēmetha, tas d’ anemos te kybernētai t’ ithynon.
sentences.l:
But when indeed the third day fine-plaited Dawn brought to its end,
masts having set up and sails, white, having hoisted,
we sat, and them the wind and the helmsmen guided straight.
sentences.i: But when fine-plaited Dawn had brought the third day round, we set up the masts and hoisted the white sails and sat, and the wind and the helmsmen kept the ships straight on their course.
sentences.n: τέλεσ’ is ἐτέλεσε 'brought to completion', with τρίτον ἦμαρ its object and ἐυπλόκαμος Ἠώς the subject. ἱστοὺς στησάμενοι is 'having set up the masts', and ἀνά … ἐρύσαντες is tmesis, 'drawing up' the sails; λεύκ’ is λευκά 'white'. ἥμεθα is 'we sat', from ἧμαι: with the wind doing the work, the men only sit. τάς is the pronoun 'them', the ships. ἴθυνον is an unaugmented imperfect of ἰθύνω 'keep straight', and κυβερνῆται are the steersmen.

sentences.t: καί νύ κεν ἀσκηθὴς ἱκόμην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν·
sentences.tr: kai ny ken askēthēs hikomēn es patrida gaian·
sentences.l: And now, unharmed I would have come to my fatherland;
sentences.i: And I would surely have reached my fatherland unharmed;
sentences.n: κε(ν) is Homeric ἄν. Here it stands with the aorist ἱκόμην and makes a past that did not come true, 'I would have arrived'. καί νύ is 'and now, and so'. ἀσκηθής is 'unharmed'. ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν is 'to my fatherland', and the raised point prepares the ἀλλά that overturns it.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά με κῦμα ῥόος τε περιγνάμπτοντα Μάλειαν
καὶ Βορέης ἀπέωσε, παρέπλαγξεν δὲ Κυθήρων.
sentences.tr:
alla me kyma rhoos te perignamptonta Maleian
kai Boreēs apeōse, pareplanxen de Kythērōn.
sentences.l:
but me wave and current, rounding Malea,
and the North Wind pushed off, and drove astray from Cythera.
sentences.i: but as I was rounding Malea, the wave and the current and the North Wind thrust me off and drove me astray from Cythera.
sentences.n: ἀπέωσε is the aorist of ἀπωθέω 'thrust away', and its three subjects, κῦμα ῥόος τε … καὶ Βορέης, share the one verb. περιγνάμπτοντα is a participle agreeing with με, 'as I rounded'. Μάλεια is the cape at the southeast of the Peloponnese, and Κύθηρα an island off it. παρέπλαγξεν is the aorist of παραπλάζω 'drive astray past', and Κυθήρων a genitive of separation, 'away from Cythera'.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν δ’ ἐννῆμαρ φερόμην ὀλοοῖς ἀνέμοισιν
πόντον ἐπ’ ἰχθυόεντα·
sentences.tr:
enthen d’ ennēmar pheromēn oloois anemoisin
ponton ep’ ichthyoenta·
sentences.l:
From there for nine days I was carried by deadly winds
over the fish-teeming open-sea;
sentences.i: From there for nine days I was carried by deadly winds over the fish-teeming sea;
sentences.n: ἐννῆμαρ is 'for nine days'. φερόμην is the passive imperfect 'I was carried'. ὀλοοῖς ἀνέμοισιν is a dative plural in -οισι: ὀλοός is 'destructive, deadly'. ἐπ’ … ἰχθυόεντα is 'over the fish-teeming sea', ἰχθυόεις being 'full of fish', a stock epithet. A new paragraph begins, and the unit ends mid-line at the raised point.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ δεκάτῃ ἐπέβημεν
γαίης Λωτοφάγων, οἵ τ’ ἄνθινον εἶδαρ ἔδουσιν.
sentences.tr:
atar dekatēi epebēmen
gaiēs Lōtophagōn, hoi t’ anthinon eidar edousin.
sentences.l:
but on the tenth we set foot
on the land of the Lotus-eaters, who flowery food eat.
sentences.i: and on the tenth day we set foot on the land of the Lotus-eaters, who eat a flowery food.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ is 'but, and then'. δεκάτῃ is a dative of time, 'on the tenth', ἡμέρα being understood. ἐπέβημεν is the aorist of ἐπιβαίνω 'set foot on', with the genitive γαίης. Λωτοφάγων is the genitive plural of Λωτοφάγος, from λωτός and φαγεῖν 'eat'; the name says what they eat, but which plant λωτός is, is not known. οἵ τ’ is οἵ τε, with the epic τε of a habit. ἄνθινον εἶδαρ is 'flowery food', εἶδαρ being a rare word for food, and ἔδουσιν is uncontracted 'they eat'.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἐπ’ ἠπείρου βῆμεν καὶ ἀφυσσάμεθ’ ὕδωρ,
αἶψα δὲ δεῖπνον ἕλοντο θοῇς παρὰ νηυσὶν ἑταῖροι.
sentences.tr:
entha d’ ep’ ēpeirou bēmen kai aphyssameth’ hydōr,
aipsa de deipnon helonto thoēis para nēusin hetairoi.
sentences.l:
And there onto the mainland we went and drew water,
and quickly a meal took, by the swift ships, the companions.
sentences.i: There we went up onto the mainland and drew water, and my companions quickly took their meal beside the swift ships.
sentences.n: βῆμεν is an old aorist of βαίνω, 'we went'. ἠπείρου is the mainland, in contrast with the sea. ἀφυσσάμεθ’ is the aorist middle of ἀφύσσω 'draw', the verb used for liquids. αἶψα is 'quickly'. δεῖπνον ἕλοντο is 'took a meal', the aorist middle of αἱρέω. In θοῇς παρὰ νηυσίν the preposition stands between adjective and noun, and ἑταῖροι, the subject, comes last.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ σίτοιό τ’ ἐπασσάμεθ’ ἠδὲ ποτῆτος,
δὴ τότ’ ἐγὼν ἑτάρους προΐειν πεύθεσθαι ἰόντας,
οἵ τινες ἀνέρες εἶεν ἐπὶ χθονὶ σῖτον ἔδοντες
ἄνδρε δύω κρίνας, τρίτατον κήρυχ’ ἅμ’ ὀπάσσας.
sentences.tr:
autar epei sitoio t’ epassameth’ ēde potētos,
dē tot’ egōn hetarous proïein peuthesthai iontas,
hoi tines aneres eien epi chthoni siton edontes
andre dyō krinas, tritaton kērych’ ham’ opassas.
sentences.l:
But when of food and of drink we had partaken,
then I companions sent forth to inquire, going,
who the men might be, on the earth eating bread,
two men choosing, and a third, a herald, along with them adding.
sentences.i: But when we had partaken of food and drink, I sent some of my companions to go and find out who the men were who ate bread on the earth, choosing two men and adding a herald as a third.
sentences.n: ἐπασσάμεθ’ is the aorist middle of πατέομαι 'partake of', with the genitives σίτοιο and ποτῆτος. ἐγών is ἐγώ. προΐειν is an imperfect of προΐημι, 'I sent forward'. πεύθεσθαι ἰόντας is 'to learn, going', an infinitive of purpose. οἵ τινες ἀνέρες εἶεν is an indirect question, 'who the men were', with the optative because the main verb is past; ἀνέρες is ἄνδρες. σῖτον ἔδοντες 'eating bread' marks civilised men. ἄνδρε and δύω are dual, and τρίτατον 'as a third' agrees with κήρυχ’. κήρυχ’ is κήρυκα 'herald', and ὀπάσσας is the aorist participle of ὀπάζω 'add as a companion'.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ αἶψ’ οἰχόμενοι μίγεν ἀνδράσι Λωτοφάγοισιν·
sentences.tr: hoi d’ aips’ oichomenoi migen andrasi Lōtophagoisin·
sentences.l: And they, quickly going off, mingled with the men, Lotus-eaters;
sentences.i: They soon went off and mingled with the Lotus-eating men;
sentences.n: οἰχόμενοι is 'going off', from οἴχομαι. μίγεν is the aorist passive of μίγνυμι without augment (= ἐμίγησαν), 'they mingled with', and takes the dative ἀνδράσι Λωτοφάγοισιν, in -οισιν. The word stands for going among them and joining them.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα Λωτοφάγοι μήδονθ’ ἑτάροισιν ὄλεθρον
ἡμετέροις, ἀλλά σφι δόσαν λωτοῖο πάσασθαι.
sentences.tr:
oud’ ara Lōtophagoi mēdonth’ hetaroisin olethron
hēmeterois, alla sphi dosan lōtoio pasasthai.
sentences.l:
And not the Lotus-eaters planned for companions destruction,
ours, but gave them of lotus to taste.
sentences.i: And the Lotus-eaters did not plan destruction for my companions, but gave them lotus to taste.
sentences.n: μήδονθ’ is ἐμήδοντο, an imperfect of μήδομαι 'plan', with θ before the breathing of the next word. ὄλεθρον is 'destruction'; ἑτάροισιν ἡμετέροις is 'our companions', a dative plural in -οισιν. δόσαν is the unaugmented aorist 'they gave'. λωτοῖο πάσασθαι is 'to taste of lotus': the genitive is partitive and πάσασθαι the aorist infinitive of πατέομαι. The harm comes from a welcome, not from hostility.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ὅς τις λωτοῖο φάγοι μελιηδέα καρπόν,
οὐκέτ’ ἀπαγγεῖλαι πάλιν ἤθελεν οὐδὲ νέεσθαι,
ἀλλ’ αὐτοῦ βούλοντο μετ’ ἀνδράσι Λωτοφάγοισι
λωτὸν ἐρεπτόμενοι μενέμεν νόστου τε λαθέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
tōn d’ hos tis lōtoio phagoi meliēdea karpon,
ouket’ apangeilai palin ēthelen oude neesthai,
all’ autou boulonto met’ andrasi Lōtophagoisi
lōton ereptomenoi menemen nostou te lathesthai.
sentences.l:
But of them whoever the honey-sweet fruit of the lotus ate,
no longer to bring back word wished, nor to return,
but right there they wanted, among the men, the Lotus-eaters,
feeding on lotus, to remain and of homecoming to forget.
sentences.i: But whoever among them ate the honey-sweet fruit of the lotus no longer wished to bring back word or to return, but they wanted to stay right there among the Lotus-eating men, feeding on lotus, and to forget their homecoming.
sentences.n: ὅς τις … φάγοι is 'whoever ate', with an optative for a repeated event in the past. μελιηδέα is 'honey-sweet'. ἀπαγγεῖλαι is an aorist infinitive 'report back', and νέεσθαι is uncontracted (Attic νεῖσθαι) 'to go back'. The subject changes from singular (ἤθελεν) to plural (βούλοντο), as 'whoever' becomes 'they'. αὐτοῦ is 'right there'. ἐρεπτόμενοι 'feeding on' is from ἐρέπτομαι, and μενέμεν an infinitive in -έμεν. λαθέσθαι, the aorist infinitive of λανθάνομαι 'forget', takes the genitive νόστου. The fruit takes away the wish to go home.

sentences.t:
τοὺς μὲν ἐγὼν ἐπὶ νῆας ἄγον κλαίοντας ἀνάγκῃ,
νηυσὶ δ’ ἐνὶ γλαφυρῇσιν ὑπὸ ζυγὰ δῆσα ἐρύσσας.
sentences.tr:
tous men egōn epi nēas agon klaiontas anankēi,
nēusi d’ eni glaphyrēisin hypo zyga dēsa eryssas.
sentences.l:
These I to the ships led, weeping, by force,
and in the hollow ships under the benches bound them, dragging.
sentences.i: I led these men back to the ships, weeping, by force, and dragged them under the benches of the hollow ships and bound them.
sentences.n: τοὺς μέν is 'these, for my part', and prepares τοὺς ἄλλους in the next unit. ἄγον is an imperfect, 'I was leading'. ἀνάγκῃ is a dative, 'by compulsion'. γλαφυρῇσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσιν, and ἐνί follows νηυσί. ζυγά are the ship's cross-benches, and δῆσα is the unaugmented aorist of δέω 'bind'. ἐρύσσας is the aorist participle 'dragging'; the double σ is a metrical convenience.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ τοὺς ἄλλους κελόμην ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους
σπερχομένους νηῶν ἐπιβαινέμεν ὠκειάων,
μή πώς τις λωτοῖο φαγὼν νόστοιο λάθηται.
sentences.tr:
autar tous allous kelomēn eriēras hetairous
sperchomenous nēōn epibainemen ōkeiaōn,
mē pōs tis lōtoio phagōn nostoio lathētai.
sentences.l:
And the others I ordered, my trusty companions,
hastening, to go aboard the swift ships,
lest in some way anyone, lotus having eaten, of homecoming forget.
sentences.i: And I ordered the rest of my trusty companions to hurry aboard the swift ships, lest any of them eat lotus and forget his homecoming.
sentences.n: κελόμην is the imperfect middle of κέλομαι 'order, urge'. ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους is a stock phrase, 'trusty companions'; the sense of ἐρίηρος is not fully known, 'trusty' being the traditional gloss. σπερχομένους is 'hastening'. ἐπιβαινέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν with the genitive νηῶν ὠκειάων (uncontracted; ὠκύς 'swift'). μή πώς τις is 'lest in any way anyone', and λάθηται is a subjunctive with the genitive νόστοιο: the danger is the forgetting.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ αἶψ’ εἴσβαινον καὶ ἐπὶ κληῖσι καθῖζον,
ἑξῆς δ’ ἑζόμενοι πολιὴν ἅλα τύπτον ἐρετμοῖς.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ aips’ eisbainon kai epi klēisi kathizon,
hexēs d’ hezomenoi poliēn hala typton eretmois.
sentences.l:
And they quickly went aboard and on the rowing-benches sat down,
and sitting in a row, the grey sea they struck with their oars.
sentences.i: They quickly went aboard and sat down at the oarlocks, and sitting in rows, they struck the grey sea with their oars.
sentences.n: εἴσβαινον is an imperfect, 'were going aboard'. κληῖσι is a dative of κληΐς 'rowing-bench, thwart', and καθῖζον 'sat down'. ἑξῆς is 'in order, in a row', and ἑζόμενοι is a participle of ἕζομαι 'sit down'. πολιὴν ἅλα is 'the grey sea', ἅλς being the salt sea and πολιός 'grey'. ἐρετμοῖς is a dative plural of ἐρετμόν 'oar'. The speech does not end here; Odysseus goes on speaking, so the quotation carries no closing mark.
